\chapter{Naming Who Someone Is}
\label{ch:sa-roles}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what someone's role is in Sanskrit --- teacher, student, king, guest, physician --- and name the everyday meaning hiding inside two of those words.}

Complete SA-C26-physician and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[guruḥ]{\sk{गुरुः} (guruḥ) — a teacher, and the word for heavy}

\label{lesson:SA-C26-teacher}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{keśaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{गुरुः}}
\textbf{\sk{गुरुः}} (\emph{guruḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a teacher, and the word for heavy\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{गुरुः}} reached English on its own, so you already say it. What English lost on the way is the ordinary meaning: \emph{guru} first of all means \textbf{heavy}. A heavy stone is \emph{guru}; a teacher is \emph{guru} because a teacher has weight.

The heavy-word travelled: Latin \emph{gravis} — whence \emph{grave}, \emph{gravity}, \emph{aggravate} — and Greek \emph{barus}, whence \emph{barometer}, the weight-measurer. So \sk{गुरुः}, \emph{gravity} and \emph{barometer} all descend from one word for heaviness, and only Sanskrit made a person out of it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word you already knew in English, returned to its first meaning.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{guruḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{guruḥ}, and say both of its meanings
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{गुरुः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a teacher, and the word for heavy\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śiṣyaḥ]{\sk{शिष्यः} (śiṣyaḥ) — a student, a disciple}

\label{lesson:SA-C26-student}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{guruḥ} mean, and what did it mean before that?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शिष्यः}}
\textbf{\sk{शिष्यः}} (\emph{śiṣyaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a student, a disciple\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{शिष्यः}} stands opposite \sk{गुरुः}. It is built from a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to instruct\textquotedblright{}, in a form that means \emph{one who is to be taught} — not a person who studies, but a person who is owed teaching. The obligation points at the teacher.

English arrived at the same idea by another road: \emph{disciple} is from Latin \emph{discere}, \textquotedblleft{}to learn\textquotedblright{}. Two languages, two independent words, one relationship. Masculine \textbf{-\sk{अः}}, like \sk{गुरुः}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The pair: the one with weight, and the one who is owed teaching.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śiṣyaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{guruḥ}, then \emph{śiṣyaḥ}, and say which one is owed something
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{शिष्यः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a student, a disciple\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rājā]{\sk{राजा} (rājā) — a king}

\label{lesson:SA-C26-king}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{śiṣyaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{राजा}}
\textbf{\sk{राजा}} (\emph{rājā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a king\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{राजा}} is a king, and it belongs to the same \emph{-\sk{ऋ}}-shaped family as \sk{पिता} and \sk{माता} — the stem is \emph{rājan-}.

Its cousin in Rome is \emph{rēx}, in its other forms \emph{rēgem}: \emph{regal}, \emph{royal}, \emph{regent}, \emph{rex}. In Gaul, chieftains' names ended in \emph{-rīx} — Vercingetorix. English borrowed \emph{raj} and \emph{maharaja} back from India in the nineteenth century, so the word has now entered English twice, three thousand years apart, by two different doors.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One word, two arrivals in English, with millennia between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rājā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{rājā}, then \emph{pitā}, and name the family both stems share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{राजा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a king\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[atithiḥ]{\sk{अतिथिः} (atithiḥ) — a guest}

\label{lesson:SA-C26-guest}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{rājā} mean, and what did \emph{guruḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{अतिथिः}}
\textbf{\sk{अतिथिः}} (\emph{atithiḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{अतिथिः}} is a guest. Tradition reads the word as \emph{a-tithi}, \textquotedblleft{}one without a date\textquotedblright{} — the visitor who arrives unannounced, on no appointed day, and must be fed anyway. Linguists prefer a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}to wander\textquotedblright{} and derive it as \textquotedblleft{}the wanderer\textquotedblright{}.

Keep the traditional reading; keep also the fact that it is a reading. Either way the famous line \textbf{\sk{अतिथिदेवो} \sk{भव}} — \textquotedblleft{}be one to whom the guest is a god\textquotedblright{} — tells you how much weight the word carries.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four roles, and one of them arrives without warning.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{atithiḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{atithiḥ}, and say what the traditional reading claims
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{अतिथिः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vaidyaḥ]{\sk{वैद्यः} (vaidyaḥ) — a physician}

\label{lesson:SA-C26-physician}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of this run: what did \emph{atithiḥ} mean, and what did \emph{śiṣyaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{वैद्यः}}
\textbf{\sk{वैद्यः}} (\emph{vaidyaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a physician\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{वैद्यः}} is a physician — literally \emph{one who has the knowledge}, built on \emph{vidyā}, knowledge, from a root \emph{vid}, \textquotedblleft{}to know\textquotedblright{}.

That root is one of the great travellers: Latin \emph{vidēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} — \emph{video}, \emph{evident}; Greek \emph{idea}; English \emph{wit}, \emph{wise}, \emph{wisdom}. And Sanskrit already gave you a second knowing-verb, \sk{जानाति}, from a different root altogether. Sanskrit keeps two ways of knowing apart, and \sk{वैद्यः} belongs to the one that also means seeing — the doctor as the one who has looked.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five roles: teacher, student, king, guest, physician.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vaidyaḥ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, and name the two that make a pair
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{वैद्यः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a physician\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
